newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Schmidhuber-ECB bound to uphold stability.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Schmidhuber-ECB bound to uphold stability.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Peter Schmidhuber said on Wednesday the European Central Bank was bound to uphold the stability of the euro after the start of European currency union, set for January 1999.

"The Maastricht treaty decides in favour of stability when settling all economic conflicts of interest. The ECB is duty bound to (uphold) the stability of the currency," Schmidhuber said in the text of a speech to be delivered in Boppard, Germany.
Schmidhuber said oordination of economic policy in Europe after the start of currency union should not become a counterweight to the European Central Bank.

"The necessary coordination of economic policy cannot become a "counterweight" to the European Central Bank, but must be decided by an institution which acts as a partner to the ECB and is similarly dedicated to the stability of the currency," Schmidhuber said.
"The ECB will not allow any weighing up of the goal of stability with other economic objectives, such as growth or employment," he said.

The Maastricht treaty also put restrictions on the effects of the so-called employment pact, agreed at the EU summit in Amsterdam, in response to demands from the newly-elected socialist government in France.
"This also illustrates the limits of an employment pact. (An employment pact) has to limit itself to within the parameters of other areas of economic or fiscal policy," he said.
The debate about softening entry criteria for the European currency union or delaying the start was "premature and damaging," he said.

"This debate cannot be held at any serious level at the moment....it is premature and damaging because it reduces efforts to consolidate and at worst can have the effect of a self fulfilling prophecy."
The start of currency union should not be hampered by political concessions, which could endanger the future of the whole project.
The view that a less stable euro would lead to increased employment was an error, he said, and there could be no question of the mark being devalued when the time came to set the value of the euro.
"If one takes the EU's share of world trade as a measure, then the outlook for euro is not bad. About 40 percent of world trade is carried out by EU states," Schmidhuber said.

"If the euro is stable, then the addition of two factors -- the EU's share of world trade and the efficiency of European financial markets -- will contribute to helping form the euro as an investment, reserve and transaction medium," he said.
